content:
There are people that get AI models like Claude, chatGPT to formalize large swaths of results in Lean - in many cases without reading it themselves . From a security stand point, how safe is this?

In particular, how susceptible to LLM code-injection attacks is Lean? In other words, could someone malicious write a blog post with some malicious Lean code, and a convincing explanation of how that Lean code does this or that useful thing. Wait until it gets used and run in someone's LLM generated Lean code, and reap the benefits.

What guards do we have against this?

As for the guarantees that can be established about a Lean proof using various methods refer to https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/ValidatingProofs/. The ultimate guard for a Lean proof is https://github.com/leanprover/comparator/ which checks with a very high assurance that a solution to a particular theorem statement does in fact pass the Lean kernel (and potential alternative kernels) without any tricks.
I was thinking more on the more seriously malicious side, e.g. using the IO monad to interact with the users system.
Yes, comparator guards against this seriously malicious side

Maybe I'm confused about what comparator does, but you are saying it would prevent something like:

#eval IO.FS.removeFile "/path/of/important/file.txt"

in the middle of an AI generated formalization?

Well this is all assuming you actually run the Lean code only using comparator (which uses landrun to sandbox). Otherwise, running (and compiling) Lean code is no less and no more safe than running code written in any other programming language.

Joseph Tooby-Smith said:

Maybe I'm confused about what comparator does, but you are saying it would prevent something like:

#eval IO.FS.removeFile "/path/of/important/file.txt"

in the middle of an AI generated formalization?

As Robin says, if you actually use comparator to verify an AI formalization that you got from the internet, yes comparator will prevent this and many other tampering tricks of this kind. If you touch the code in any other way (open it in your editor, run lake build on it yourself etc.) all bets are off. Though you could of course run the code in a VM yourself and only the VM could be corrupted.

But then I worry that I don't think a large proportion of people are actually doing this, and many people are using AI directly in the code editors. Maybe all of this isn't too big of a concern right now,

When I was grading my students' Lean code about 5 years ago I took the trouble to learn about sandboxing, virtual machines etc, precisely because I was worried about this. I would definitely recommend that you don't compile a random Lean repo you find on the internet! I update and compile core Lean and mathlib happily on my machines, but I trust the maintainers of these repos.

But isn't this exactly what LLMs are doing, taking code from the internet, putting it into your code editor (indeed this is the premise of the code-injection attacks)?

But because of the way that Lean works, I think the situation is even worse. I'm using GitHub copilot: Lean runs suggestions from GitHub copilot before I've approved them. See the screen shot, where I ask it to make a file, I haven't approved the output, yet Lean has already made the file.
I think you might also be confused about what LLMs are doing. In my experience they don't "take code from the internet" unless you specifically ask them to.

Yeah, I agree. I think I mean "being trained on data from the internet e.g. Lean code on GitHub", rather than "taking code from the internet" via a web-agent (although I suspect the latter also happens).
(Also GitHub Copilot does have a switch to turn on its web-agent to improve answers).

My two cents: I generally reframe from even editing latex on my own machine now. I think we have passed the point where these models are capable enough for bad actors to effectively use to compromise the upstream of anything.

MacOS has a nice native virtualization framework btw.
I could swear there was a thread about this exact issue (sandboxing to prevent malicious AI code from touching your filesystem) with Terence Tao, does anyone know where it is?

Matthew Ballard said:

I think we have passed the point where these models are capable enough for bad actors to effectively use to compromise the upstream of anything.

I think such claims without sources can cause dangerous hubris. Just half a year ago Anthropic disagreed with you: https://www.anthropic.com/research/small-samples-poison. I think more research is needed (perhaps Anthropic are working on it) before one could claim such a thing about new models from the past 6 months.

Snir Broshi said:

I could swear there was a thread about this exact issue (sandboxing to prevent malicious AI code from touching your filesystem) with Terence Tao, does anyone know where it is?

#PrimeNumberTheorem+ > LeanCert for numerical log bounds (re: PNT#892, PNT#914) ?

To be clear, I am not saying you can point a model at code base and it will zero-day it. I am saying that is a ton of problems that people already know about (eg namesquatting, low bandwidth for review, etc) that are much easier to exploit today with help from AI for a random malcontent without technical skills.

Oh I see, I misinterpreted your original message completely, sorry, I think there's some parsing ambiguity there.
I thought you said that the models are good enough that bad actors can't cause them to behave maliciously (e.g. through training-data poisoning, as I linked), or that the models don't act maliciously anymore because alignment is solved (e.g. https://www.axios.com/2025/05/23/anthropic-ai-deception-risk).

But IIUC based on this clarification, you were talking about bad actors using LLMs to do bad things. In that case, I don't see how it relates to the current thread, the question was about LLM users affected by bad actors. But I may be wrong.
Matthew was arguing that no one should be running anything non-trivial outside of a sandbox / disposable machine, because today you have to assume that everything upstream is suspect.

But IIUC based on this clarification, you were talking about bad actors using LLMs to do bad things. In that case, I don't see how it relates to the current thread, the question was about LLM users affected by bad actors. But I may be wrong.

Yeah, my question was more about attacks where the bad guys affect good guys using the LLMs. There are a number of attacks in this direction, some described here. In particular poisoning of data, which apparently can occur on any model size, even with a small amount of poisoning.

However, I think any defenses against this would hold more widely.

Robin Arnez said:

Well this is all assuming you actually run the Lean code only using comparator (which uses landrun to sandbox).

You do need to in principle be a little wary even running code in a sandbox. Landrun has had a known hole in it for months, which is in the process of being fixed. I was able to write a .lean file that could break out of Comparator back in January, which I showed the devs privately. Henrik has since updated Comparator to block this vulnerability, but I think it's important to remember that there's really no such thing as 'absolute certainty' when it comes to these kinds of security questions.
